newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Howard signals easier media rules.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Howard signals easier media rules.

text.p: The Australian government, under strong pressure from media giants, on Thursday indicated it could ease media ownership limits.

Prime Minister John Howard, whose government is reviewing media ownership laws, said any reforms must be in the national interest but added that Australia needed a strong media company to compete internationally.
"(One) ... argument is the fact that in the modern age of convergence the idea of having cross media prohibitions is ridiculous," said Howard.

He has held a series of talks this week with leading media owners including News Corp Ltd chief Rupert Murdoch, Australia's richest man, magazine and television tycoon Kerry Packer, and Canadian television station operator Izzy Asper, the owner of the Canwest Global group.
Australia needed a "very powerful, fully Australian-based media company" to compete successfully in the Asia-Pacific region, he said in a radio interview.
"There is some national benefit in having a very powerful, fully Australian-based media company if you are to have a presence in the region and a presence around the world," he said.
"If you are to have a company that can .... be a flag-waver of Australia, then you need a very, very strong domestic base."

Murdoch, a U.S. citizen who retains extensive media interests in Australia, and Packer, whose Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd operates the Nine television network and owns a stable of magazines, have lobbied Canberra to drop laws which limit cross ownership between newspapers and
The law prevents a television operator owning more than 15 percent of a newspaper in the same market, and vice versa.
Packer's company owns 15 percent of leading newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd and analysts say abolition of the cross-ownership limits would clear the way for a takeover bid.
Canadian media baron Conrad Black, the owner of London's Daily Telegraph newspaper, last year bailed out of Fairfax because of frustrations over the media rules.
Of his 25 percent stake, 20 percent was sold directly to New Zealand's Brierley Investments Ltd.
If Brierley wanted to increase its stake to 25 percent, it would have to make a full takeover bid for the company.
Fairfax currently has a market value of about A$2.4 billion.
